summary.text: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only astronomical object known to harbor life.
It is the only planet in the Solar System with liquid water on its surface, and its ocean covers 70.8% of its crust.
A liquid outer core makes a magnetosphere that deflects most solar wind and cosmic radiation, and its atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen.

items.prompt: Many places on Earth swing between summer and winter. What causes seasons?

options.label: It moves much closer to the Sun in summer
The Moon's gravity changes the sunlight it gets
Its rotation axis is tilted relative to its orbit
Its orbit is a long, stretched oval

items.explain: The tilt of Earth's axis of rotation with respect to its orbital plane around the Sun produces seasons.

items.prompt: Water vapor and carbon dioxide in the air capture energy from sunlight. What does that make possible?

options.label: A surface temperature at which water stays liquid
A magnetic shield against the solar wind
A steady slow drift of tectonic plates
A tide that rises twice a day

items.explain: These gases capture the Sun's energy, keeping an average of 14.76 °C where water is liquid under normal pressure.

items.prompt: What does the Moon's gravity do for Earth?

options.label: It keeps Earth's outer core liquid
It pushes tectonic plates around
It speeds up Earth's rotation
It raises tides and steadies Earth's tilt

items.explain: The Moon's gravity helps stabilize Earth's axis, causes tides, and gradually slows Earth's rotation.

items.prompt: The same face of the Moon looks toward us night after night. Why?

options.label: The Moon is far too small to spin
Earth's gravity has locked the Moon's rotation to its orbit
The Sun's glare hides its far side
The Moon's magnetic field fixes it in place

items.explain: Earth's gravitational pull has made the Moon's rotation tidally locked, keeping the same near side facing Earth.

items.prompt: As life spread across the young Earth, what happened to the planet itself?

options.label: Life stayed in the ocean with no wider effect
Life changed its atmosphere and surface
Life stopped its crust from moving
Life slowed its spin around its axis

items.explain: Life spread globally and has been altering Earth's atmosphere and surface, leading to the Great Oxidation Event.

items.prompt: Lakes, rivers, groundwater and the air hold a lot of water. How much do the polar ice sheets hold in comparison?

options.label: More than all of those put together
Less than the lakes alone
About the same as the groundwater
Almost none, because ice is solid

items.explain: Large ice sheets at the polar deserts retain more water than groundwater, lakes, rivers and atmospheric water combined.

paragraphs.heading: The living planet
paragraphs.text: Earth is the third planet out from the Sun and the only place known to hold life. Life is possible here because Earth is an ocean world, and no other planet in the Solar System keeps liquid water on its surface. The ocean holds nearly all of Earth's water and covers 70.8% of the crust. The other 29.2% is dry land, gathered mostly into continents within one half of the globe, the land hemisphere.

paragraphs.heading: Moving plates and a shield
paragraphs.text: Earth's crust is split into tectonic plates that drift slowly and interact, building mountain ranges and setting off volcanoes and earthquakes. Deep inside, a liquid outer core produces a magnetosphere that turns aside most of the harmful solar wind and cosmic radiation. Above the ground, an atmosphere made mainly of nitrogen and oxygen maintains conditions at the surface. It also stops most meteoroids and ultraviolet light as they come in.

paragraphs.heading: Why the water stays liquid
paragraphs.text: Water vapor is spread widely through the air and forms clouds over most of the planet. That vapor is a greenhouse gas. Together with other greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide (CO₂), it holds on to energy from sunlight. This keeps the average surface temperature at 14.76 °C, where water stays liquid at normal air pressure. The equator gets more sunlight than the poles, and this uneven heating drives currents in the air and ocean, giving Earth its climate regions and weather such as precipitation.

paragraphs.heading: Size, orbit and seasons
paragraphs.text: Earth is rounded into an ellipsoid about 40,000 km around. It is the densest planet in the Solar System, and the biggest and heaviest of the four rocky planets. It sits about eight light-minutes, or 1 astronomical unit (AU), from the Sun and goes around it once a year, in about 365.25 days. It spins on its axis in about 23 hours and 56 minutes. That axis is tilted compared with the plane of its orbit, and the tilt gives us seasons.

paragraphs.heading: The Moon's pull
paragraphs.text: Earth has one permanent natural satellite, the Moon, which circles at 384,400 km and is about a quarter as wide as Earth. The Moon's gravity steadies Earth's axis, raises the tides and slowly brakes Earth's spin. In return, Earth's pull has tidally locked the Moon, so the same near side always faces us.

paragraphs.heading: A long history
paragraphs.text: Like most bodies in the Solar System, Earth took shape some 4.5 billion years ago out of gas and dust. The ocean appeared, and life began, within its first billion years. Life spread around the globe and changed the air and the land, which led two billion years ago to the Great Oxidation Event. Humans appeared in Africa 300,000 years ago and now live on every continent. We rely on Earth's biosphere and resources, yet our present impact on its climate and biosphere is unsustainable and is causing widespread extinctions.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word Earth came, through Middle English, from an Old English noun usually spelled eorðe. In its earliest uses it covered all the meanings of Latin terra and Greek gē, from soil and dry land to the whole globe. The name Terra still turns up now and then in scientific writing, and science fiction uses it to tell our home planet apart from others.
